8.0.0.en: At the beginning of the Song the bride began by pleading to enter into the life of fellowship with Him. She desired to be alone with Him more and more, once in the wilderness, again in the garden, a third time in the field and the villages, and a fourth time in her mother's house, to give Him to drink of the wine of her love, as He had given her to drink of His eternal love. Therefore she speaks to Him, saying:

8.0.1.en: "O that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised.

8.0.2.en: I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother's house, and the chamber of her that conceived me: thou wouldest instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of the mingled wine of the juice of my pomegranate" [1-2].

8.0.3.en: If this chapter is in essence a discourse about service, then the foundation of service, and its basis, is that the servant first enjoys the Bridegroom of the Church, so that when he meets his brethren they may smell in him the fragrance of "life" and receive membership in the Church, the body of the living Christ.

8.0.4.en: In this discourse we also notice the following: 1. She desires to kiss Him as a brother of hers, who sucked the breasts of her mother... For according to the ancient Eastern traditions it was not fitting to practice kisses openly even between a man and his wife, and none was excepted from this except the nearest relatives, such as parents and brothers. Therefore she wants Him as a brother of hers who sucked the breasts of her mother, so that she may take Him in her arms, appear with Him openly, and kiss Him in the presence of all mankind, and no one would blame her. 2. Perhaps the secret of her calling to Him with the hope, "O that thou wert as my brother...", is that she declares the longing of the Church of the Old Testament, which looked to God as One who is outside, for she says, "I should find thee without". She asks Him to come down to the human race and not remain isolated, but to become a firstborn brother by sharing our nature and dwelling in our midst, so that we may come to know Him, and receive Him with the kisses of open worship, and bring Him into our inner life. 3. It is also the discourse of the Church of the New Testament, who realized in the maturity of her love that the Lord Christ, the firstborn Brother, who is her Lord, her Master and her Bridegroom, is kissed by the believers with the kisses of living worship, and they bring Him into the house of their mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, to live with Him face to face in His eternal embrace. 4. As for her saying, "thou wouldest instruct me"..., it is a revelation of the nature of the true Christian and the faithful servant. For even if the soul meets her Bridegroom, kisses Him and lives with Him in her mother's house, the Church or the heavenly Jerusalem, and there gives Him to drink of the wine of her joy mingled with the juice of her pomegranate, yet she remains in humility, wanting to learn... She is in need of Him to teach her His heavenly mysteries, so that even in eternity, when she remains in His embrace, she sees Him constantly new in her eyes... as though from one moment to the next (if this expression is right, for in eternity there are no moments or time) she learns something new about His divine mysteries.

8.0.5.en: The true servant remains always in the Church, the house of his mother, at the feet of the Savior, asking to learn, even if he is called "teacher" or "father" by many! In this St. Ambrose says: [I wish to strive in learning so that I may be able to teach. For there is one Master (God) who alone does not learn what He teaches to all. But men must learn before they teach, and receive from God their Teacher what they teach others.] St. Jerome also says: [The mind that longs to learn deserves praise even if it has no teacher.] 5. Learning in the Church, the house of the mother, is not merely intellectual knowledge or memorizing teachings by heart, but in essence it is entering into the practice of "life with Christ". Therefore the bride says: "I would cause thee to drink of the mingled wine of the juice of my pomegranate"... This is what I learn: to return Your love with love. 6. When a person enters the Church in the company of the Lord, and here sits at the feet of the Savior learning, he offers wine mingled with the juice of the pomegranate... What does this mean? We have seen wine as a symbol of the life of joy and gladness... For the Church is the joyful house that receives repentant sinners, and the Lord gives them an inner joy and a gladness that temporal events cannot take away. As for the pomegranate, it signifies the life of spiritual striving, for the pomegranate tree is full of thorns, and its rind is bitter, and inside it are many seeds, but its juice carries a beautiful flavor and a delicious taste. So joy in Christianity is mingled with labors and spiritual striving to the end.

8.1.0.en: Finally the bride affirms her union with her Bridegroom and her attachment to Him, and repeats what she had said before:

8.1.1.en: "His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.

8.1.2.en: I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes (powers) of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please" [3-4].

8.1.3.en: These are the same words that she uttered when she declared that she was "sick of love", and we have already explained them.

8.1.4.en: Perhaps she wanted to affirm here that even though she offered all her life for service, yet in this she does not stop her fellowship with Him and her preoccupation with Him... Rather, she affirms that she will not allow anything or anyone to hinder her union with Him, for living service does not distract the servant from his Christ, but in truth leads him into deeper depths of life with Him.

8.2.s.en: The testimony of the world to Him:

8.2.0.en: As the world looks at the Church, which is the body of Christ and His witness before it, it says to her:

8.2.1.en: "Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, all white, leaning upon her beloved (her near one)?!" [5].

8.2.2.en: The daughters of Jerusalem had already uttered similar words (Song 3:6) when they saw the wonderful change in the life of the believers. Baptism had given them a heavenly whiteness, and they enjoyed a true reliance upon the Beloved, who is able to lift them up from the wilderness of this world and bring them into His heavens. Now the world marvels through the testimony of the working bride before them... She does not amaze them merely by the abundance of her work, but rather by the fruit in her life, for the appearance of the servant in the white garments of Baptism is the best testimony for the Bridegroom...

8.2.3.en: St. Augustine comments on this text saying: [She was not white from the beginning, but became white afterwards, for "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" (Isa 1:18).] He also says: [Who is this that cometh up white in the splendor of light and not with a false color?!] And St. Ambrose says: [She was black before, so how did she suddenly become white (through Baptism)?!]

8.2.4.en: And St. Augustine explains the secret of her continuing whiteness thus: [Now this one who has become white walks well, because she continues leaning upon Him who made her white. For Jesus Himself, upon whom she leans and who makes her white, says to His disciples: "Without me ye can do nothing" (Jn 15:5).]

8.2.5.en: Perhaps this amazement did not seize the world only, but overwhelmed the heavenly beings themselves as they see what the human being attains through his union with the Lord Christ in the font of Baptism, that is, they see him in his new birth bearing the possibility of ascending toward the heavens in white garments. As St. Cyril of Jerusalem described man in Baptism, saying: [The angels dance around you, saying, "Who is this that cometh up white in her garments, leaning upon her near one?" For the soul that was formerly a slave has been adopted by her Master and made near to Him.] The heavenly beings also repeat the following saying:

8.2.6.en: "I raised thee up (lifted thee) under the apple tree: there thy mother brought thee forth: there she brought thee forth that bare thee" [5].

8.2.7.en: This is the secret of her coming up from the wilderness all white, leaning upon her beloved: that her mother brought her forth and she that bare her gave her birth under the apple tree.

8.2.8.en: We have seen before that the "apple tree" signifies the divine Incarnation, for the Lord appeared "as the apple tree among the trees of the wood" (Song 2:3). Through the divine Incarnation the Mother Church was able to bear children to God in Baptism, able to rise toward the heavens through the incarnate God... This is the new birth, and this is its power in the life of the believers.

8.2.9.en: Here there is a link between the divine Incarnation and our spiritual birth, for the Lord was born bodily so that we may be born spiritually. And this is the secret of celebrating the feasts of the Nativity and of Baptism (Theophany) on one day in the early Church..., for the two feasts are bound together in the mind of the Church.

8.3.s.en: Not being preoccupied with service at the expense of the Bridegroom:

8.3.0.en: The working bride affirms her clinging to her Bridegroom in the midst of her preoccupation with serving her neighbor, saying:

8.3.1.en: "Set me as a seal (stamp) upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave (the tomb).

8.3.2.en: The coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame of the Lord.

8.3.3.en: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.

8.3.4.en: If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned" [6-7].

8.3.5.en: If the soul has enjoyed the new birth under the apple tree through Baptism, and in the sacrament of the Myron was sealed with the seal of the Holy Spirit, so that she became the possession of the Bridegroom, bearing His seal and His marks, then she cherishes this seal which has become hers in every aspect of her life. This life kindles the flame of her love toward Him, so she asks Him not merely to receive her between His arms or to take her in His eternal embrace, but she longs to cling to Him like a seal upon His heart and His arm, that not even death may separate her from Him!

8.3.6.en: She asks to be a seal upon the heart of the Bridegroom. She does not ask merely to have a place in His heart, but to occupy the whole heart, as though God were preoccupied with her alone. She wants not that her name be engraved upon His heart, but that she with all her life be sealed upon it, so that no one can approach or erase her name from before the face of God.

8.3.7.en: In the book of the prophet Isaiah the Lord says: "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands" (Isa 49:16), but here the bride asks to be a seal upon His arm...

8.3.8.en: Thus the bride settles in the heart of God, "the center of affection and love", and in His arm, "the center of work", resting forever upon the throne of His love and upon the seat of His power! This is the boldness of the Church before her Bridegroom!

8.3.9.en: The secret of this strong boldness is the love which the Lord has poured into our hearts toward Him. Therefore she says: "Love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave..." as though she were saying to Him: Death is trivial, it cannot separate me from my love for You, and the many waters and all the floods cannot quench it or drown it. As the Apostle Paul says: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?... For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom 8:38-39).

8.3.10.en: St. Augustine says: [The storms of the world or the waves of trials cannot quench the flame of love. Of this it was said: "Love is strong as death". For just as when death comes there is none who can resist it, since those who are born to die cannot repel the violence of death by any art or any kind of medicine, so the world cannot stand against the power of love.

8.3.11.en: He took the comparison from the example of death, its opposite: as death is violent in destroying, so love is strong in rescuing (saving).

8.3.12.en: Through love many have died to the world that they might live to God.]

8.3.13.en: In the midst of the world the bride offered to her Bridegroom what the world cannot resist; she offered her heart to Him who finds His delight in the heart. She did not stop at the limits of offering service, striving and vigils, but first offered her heart, that is, all her "love", of which she says: "If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned". It is as though she were repeating what the Apostle Paul said: "Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing" (1 Cor 13:3).

8.3.14.en: She is not like the wife who thinks she serves her husband well, so she spends all her effort in serving the house and gives him her body... but her heart is not with him! She offers the heart first, and through it she cannot refrain from serving him!

8.4.s.en: Her love for her Bridegroom kindles her love for her brethren:

8.4.0.en: When she offered all her love to the Lord, her heart was enlarged for her brethren, so she rose to seek on their behalf, saying:

8.4.1.en: "We have a little sister, and she hath no breasts:

8.4.2.en: what shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for?!

8.4.3.en: If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she be a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.

8.4.4.en: I am a wall, and my breasts like towers: then was I in his eyes as one that found peace" [8-10].

8.4.5.en: These simple expressions carry a constitution for the life of service, whose articles are summarized in the following points: 1. Realizing the position of unbelievers in relation to the Church, that they represent the "little sister", who is not only her sister, but is a sister to the Bridegroom as well as to the bride. In this view the Church does not deal with unbelievers, even those who trouble her or oppose the truth... even if they are atheists, on the level of a teacher with a pupil, but rather of the elder sister who is gentle with the younger. The younger sister may wrong the elder, so let the other bear with her because she is "the elder", and let her give her an excuse because the younger "hath no breasts"... that is, she has not discovered the truth through the two Testaments. 2. The secret of the weakness of the younger is that she has no breasts, so the work of the elder is to offer the word of God, that is, the Old and New Testaments, so that the little sister may taste them and love them and acquire them as her two breasts. This is the evangelistic work of the Church... offering the living word of God to every person. 3. What does the Church do for the little sister, when the Bridegroom has sought her as one betrothed, and she is without breasts?! Let her deal with her with all sympathy and love, not reproaching her or wounding her feelings, but being gentle with her and offering her every possibility. For if the younger be a wall, she builds upon her a palace of silver, and if she be a door, she encloses her with boards of cedar... She supports her with positive work.

8.4.6.en: The elder sister offers herself and her life to the younger, saying to her: If you are in need of a wall to surround you and two towers to lift you up... I am at your service: "I am a wall, and my breasts like towers". Receive the Lord Christ who is within me as a wall for you, and my Holy Bible as two breasts to satisfy you. 4. The matter does not stop at treating what is lacking in the life of the little sister who has no breasts, but the elder builds upon her a palace of silver and encloses her with boards of cedar... as though she supports her sister until she becomes a working servant in the vineyard of the Lord. The work of the Church is to bring unbelievers into the faith and urge them to practical witness to the word of God before others... Thus they become like the palace of silver (silver signifies the word of God refined like silver, and the palace signifies open witness).

8.4.7.en: Thus the Church becomes in the eyes of all as one that found true peace in the life of mankind.

8.5.0.en: "Solomon had a vineyard at Baalhamon; he let out the vineyard unto keepers (guards); every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver. My vineyard, which is mine, is before me: thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred.

8.5.1.en: Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it.

8.5.2.en: Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart (a young one) upon the mountains of spices" [11-14]. 1. As the Church enters with the world to her Bridegroom the Lord Christ... she calls all to enjoy Him, and here the Church makes clear an important principle in service: the vineyard is the vineyard of Christ, and He is the one who works in it through the vinedressers. Therefore she says: "Solomon had a vineyard at Baalhamon". The vineyard is not her vineyard, but the vineyard of the "true Solomon"...

8.5.3.en: In this St. Augustine says: [God cultivates us, His vineyard... Our planting is the work that is in our hearts, and He does not work with human hands. He cultivates us as the husbandman does his field. The Lord says in the Gospel: "I am the vine, ye are the branches... my Father is the husbandman" (Jn 15:1, 5). And what does the husbandman do? He cultivates his field. So God the Father is a husbandman who has a field which He cultivates, and from which He expects fruit. And the Lord Jesus Christ Himself says that a man "planted a vineyard... and let it out to husbandmen"; these are bound to render the fruits in their seasons.]

8.5.4.en: St. John Chrysostom also says, commenting on the saying of the Apostle: ["For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building" (1 Cor 3:9)... The field is not ascribed to him who sows in it but to its owner.] 2. The word "Baal" means "lord" or "king", and "Hamon" means "multitude". It is as though the vineyard of the Lord Christ, the King of Peace, is the multitudes of mankind... He becomes King of these multitudes to bring them into His heavens. 3. The Lord has let out this vineyard to vinedressers... "he let out the vineyard unto keepers", but He does not cease to care for the vineyard Himself and to look after it in great love, for He says, "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me". He guards it Himself night and day (Isa 27:1-3), and does not withhold anything from it, even saying in reproach: "Judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it?!" (Isa 5:3-4). 4. What is the fruit that the King of Peace asks for? "Every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver". This is what He asks of the vinedressers, that all bring thousands, because the thousand signifies heaven and the heavenly life. For God will accept from the servants only spiritual, heavenly fruit. This is the work of the Church and the mission of the servants of the word... to bring those they serve into the heavenly life. 5. If the fruit is rendered for the account of the Lord Christ, what is the share of the servants? "Thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred". Perhaps by the two hundred he meant one hundred for the men of the Old Testament and one hundred for the men of the New Testament, for the fruit is abundant and all the servants in both Testaments enjoy it. Therefore the Apostle Paul says to his people: "my joy and crown" (Phil 4:1). 6. As the Church works in the vineyard of the Lord, and the workers realize that they work for the account of the Lord Christ, who has "the thousand", and also for their own account, for they have "the two hundred", they become like those who are in the midst of gardens. The narrow gate and the afflicted way are transformed into an easy yoke and a light burden. They live while on earth as in joyful paradises, so the Lord speaks to His bride, saying: "Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it". The voice of your love is no longer muffled, but those on earth hear it, as the heavenly beings rejoice in it... And now come to Me that I may hear your joyful, practical voice, come, "inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" (Mt 25:34).

8.5.5.en: These are the words of a Bridegroom who gladdens the heart of His bride, and assures her that what she does will receive its fruits on an eternal level.

8.5.6.en: She answers Him with joy, saying: "Make haste (hurry), my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart (a young one) upon the mountains of spices". We have already seen why the Church likens her Bridegroom to the roe and to the young harts... Here she responds to His call, saying: Hasten to me and come, for I long for You... If You call me to meet You that You may hear my voice, then I also need to meet You.

8.5.7.en: And perhaps His coming in haste upon the mountain of spices reminds us of the spices with which the Lord was shrouded, for He meets her through her burial with Him... as she dies with Him every day, that she may live with Him forever.

8.5.8.en: This is the conclusion of the Song... as though she were repeating what the bride said in the book of the Apocalypse (Revelation): "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus"!
